nameStory: The red-fringed emerald gets its charming name from the delicate reddish-pink fringe along the edges of its otherwise emerald-green wings. This tiny moth also goes by "two-striped emerald" because of the pair of thin lines that often cross its wings, giving it a second identity depending on which feature catches your eye first.
description: The red-fringed emerald is a delicate little moth with a wingspan of about 22mm - roughly the size of a quarter. Its wings are a soft emerald or jade green color, creating beautiful camouflage against leaves. The most distinctive feature is the reddish-pink fringe that borders the wing edges, making it look like nature decorated this tiny moth with colorful trim. These moths belong to the geometer family, known for their looping caterpillars that "measure" the earth as they crawl.

idTips.label: Reddish-pink wing fringe
idTips.description: Look for the delicate pinkish-red border along all wing edges - this colorful trim stands out beautifully against the green wings and is visible even when the moth is at rest

idTips.label: Emerald green wings
idTips.description: Wings are soft jade or emerald green, often with a slightly powdery texture that can rub off on your fingers if handled

idTips.label: Quarter-sized wingspan
idTips.description: Small moth with wings spanning about 22mm - roughly the diameter of a quarter when fully spread

idTips.label: Two thin stripes
idTips.description: Often shows a pair of faint, thin lines crossing the forewings, though these may be subtle or absent in some individuals

idTips.label: Rests with wings spread
idTips.description: Unlike many moths that fold wings tent-like, geometers typically rest with wings held out horizontally against surfaces

habitat: Red-fringed emeralds can be found in a variety of wooded habitats throughout New England, from deciduous forests to mixed woodlands and forest edges. They're often attracted to porch lights and outdoor lighting near wooded areas, making suburban locations with mature trees good spots for observation. Look for them in gardens, parks, and anywhere with abundant vegetation that supports their caterpillars.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in May in New England, with fresh individuals appearing at lights and on vegetation as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs through June and July, with a possible second generation appearing in late summer. This is the best time to spot them at outdoor lights.
seasonality.fall: In warmer years, some individuals may persist into early fall, but activity generally winds down by late August in northern New England.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity; the species overwinters in an immature stage, likely as eggs or pupae hidden in leaf litter or soil.

funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, red-fringed emeralds are surprisingly widespread travelers - they can be found from the chilly forests of New Brunswick all the way to sunny Florida, and even make it to California's coast, making them one of the most geographically ambitious little green moths in North America!
confusionNotes: Red-fringed emeralds can be confused with other small green moths, but the distinctive reddish-pink wing fringe is usually diagnostic. Remember: "Pink fringe means emerald" - other green geometers typically have white, yellow, or matching green fringes.
contextualKnowledge: The name "geometer" comes from Greek meaning "earth measurer" - referring to how the caterpillars of this family move by arching their backs in loops, appearing to measure distances as they crawl. Adult geometer moths are generally recognized by their habit of resting with wings spread horizontally rather than folded.
compareHints: Since this is the only Nemoria species documented in New England, compare it with other small green geometer moths in the region. The red-fringed emerald's distinctive pinkish fringe sets it apart from similar species like the Southern Emerald or other green geometers, which typically have white or pale yellow fringes. The combination of bright emerald color and contrasting pink trim makes this species relatively easy to identify among New England's green moths.
